title: Feastables
hook: The biggest creator on YouTube launched a chocolate bar. Within three years it earned more than his videos.
situation: MrBeast’s videos cost millions to make and earned mostly from advertising, which barely covered production. His first food venture, MrBeast Burger, had run into quality problems and legal disputes.
exchange: Jimmy Donaldson launched Feastables in January 2022 with simple chocolate bars, promoted through his videos and challenges, then built distribution through Walmart, Target and other retailers.
brought: MrBeast
The largest audience on YouTube and a way of making a product part of the entertainment.
Retail partners
Shelf space across the United States and beyond.
turning_point: An investor presentation reported in 2025 showed Feastables made about $250 million in sales in 2024 and turned a profit, while the media business lost money. The product had become the business.
measure: Sales from an investor presentation reported by Fortune and Tubefilter. Not audited publicly
evidence: The figures come from a leaked investor deck reported by several outlets. They show the scale and the balance between products and media, though the company has not published accounts.
lesson: An audience pays for content once and for a product every week. Creators with retail partners turn attention into a repeat purchase.
take: Feastables is the end point of the creator economy so far: the videos are the marketing, and the chocolate pays for them. Burger taught the lesson Feastables applied, which is to own the product properly.

title: Ipsy
hook: She taught millions to do their make-up on YouTube. Then she sent them a bag of products every month.
situation: Beauty tutorials were among YouTube’s most watched videos, and beauty brands paid creators to feature products. Few creators owned the business that profited from their recommendations.
exchange: Michelle Phan, one of YouTube’s first beauty stars, co-founded Ipsy in 2011, a monthly subscription that sent subscribers a bag of sample-sized products chosen for them.
brought: Michelle Phan
Millions of viewers who trusted her taste and a deep network of beauty creators.
Brands
Products supplied for the bags, in return for reaching an engaged audience.
turning_point: Ipsy raised $100 million in 2015, valuing it at about $500 million, and by 2017 was reported to have about $500 million in annual revenue, with creators at the centre of its marketing.
measure: Revenue reported by Bloomberg and The Business of Fashion, not published by the company
evidence: Funding and revenue figures were widely reported. Phan later stepped back from the company, so the figures reflect a business she founded rather than one she ran throughout.
lesson: Creators can own the shop, not just the recommendation. A subscription turns trust into recurring revenue.
take: Phan was early to the idea that a creator’s audience is a customer base. Ipsy made recommendation a business model, with other creators as its sales force.
impact_source: Read about Ipsy’s revenue · The Business of Fashion
how_to_measure: For a subscription, track monthly churn and the share of subscribers who first arrived through creator content.

title: From Blog to Supermarket Shelf
hook: A student started a recipe blog while learning to cook differently. It became one of Britain’s best-known plant-based brands.
situation: Plant-based food was a niche in British supermarkets. Cookery books came from television chefs, and food brands from food companies.
exchange: Ella Mills started Deliciously Ella in 2012 as a blog of plant-based recipes, written while she changed her diet after illness. It grew into cookbooks, an app, a deli and then packaged food.
brought: Ella Mills
Recipes, honesty about why she started and a loyal community of readers.
Retail partners
Supermarket shelf space for snacks and meals under her name.
turning_point: Her first cookbook, in 2015, was a bestseller, and Deliciously Ella products went on sale in major supermarkets. A blog had become a brand sold far beyond its readers.
measure: A date. Company revenue has been reported in interviews rather than published consistently
evidence: The journey from blog to brand is documented by Retail Week and in her own accounts. Revenue figures in the press vary, so the case rests on the record of what was built.
lesson: A creator’s brand can outgrow the creator’s channel. Build products the audience would buy without the content, too.
take: Deliciously Ella is the British template for creator to consumer brand. It worked because the products made sense on a supermarket shelf, not only on a blog.

impact_source: Read how she went from blogger to brand owner · Retail Week
how_to_measure: For a creator food brand, track rate of sale per store against category averages, and repeat purchase from shoppers outside the creator’s audience.

title: Huda Beauty
hook: A make-up artist in Dubai started with false lashes and a blog. Investors later valued her company at more than a billion dollars.
situation: Global beauty brands were built in Paris and New York. A make-up artist with a blog in Dubai had no obvious route to an international brand.
exchange: Huda Kattan wrote a beauty blog and posted tutorials on Instagram, then launched false eyelashes under the Huda Beauty name in 2013, funded with a loan from her sister.
brought: Huda Kattan
Expertise, an enormous Instagram following and instinct for what her audience wanted.
Retailers
Distribution through Sephora and others that took the brand worldwide.
turning_point: In December 2017 TSG Consumer Partners bought a minority stake, in a deal reported to value Huda Beauty at about $1.2 billion. In 2025 Kattan bought back full ownership.
measure: A valuation reported by the press. The company did not confirm it
evidence: The investment and the buy-back are documented. The valuation is reported rather than confirmed, and revenue is not published.
deal_value: Minority stake to TSG Consumer Partners, reported valuation about $1.2 billion
lesson: Creators outside the usual places can build global brands. Distribution partners are what turn a following into a business.
take: Huda Beauty shows a creator building a global brand from Dubai, then taking it back. Ownership was the point from the start.

title: Glossier
hook: A beauty blog asked readers what they wanted. Its founder built the products and a company worth $1.8 billion.
situation: Beauty brands decided what to sell and advertised it. Customers were rarely asked before a product was made.
exchange: Emily Weiss founded Into the Gloss in 2010, interviewing women about their routines. In 2014 she launched Glossier, products shaped by readers’ comments and sold directly online.
brought: Emily Weiss and Into the Gloss
An engaged readership and years of conversation about what people wanted.
Investors
Funding to build products, shops and a brand around the community.
turning_point: Glossier raised $80 million in July 2021 at a $1.8 billion valuation. The company later cut staff and reset, and Weiss stepped back as chief executive in 2022.
metric_label: Valuation at the July 2021 funding round
measure: A valuation from a private funding round, reported by Retail Brew and others
evidence: The funding and valuation are documented. The later restructuring shows how hard it is to hold a community-born brand’s value at scale.
deal_value: $80 million raised at a $1.8 billion valuation, July 2021
lesson: Listen to the community before building. A product shaped by its first customers has a head start.
take: Glossier is the community-first brand everyone copied. Its later struggles are a lesson too: what a community loves at 100,000 customers can be hard to keep at ten million.

title: Kylie Cosmetics
hook: Her lip kits sold out in minutes, sold only through her own posts. Four years later Coty paid $600 million for most of the company.
situation: Celebrity beauty lines usually licensed a famous name to an established company. Few were sold mainly through the celebrity’s own social media.
exchange: Kylie Jenner launched lip kits in November 2015, announcing them on Instagram and Snapchat and selling them online, with a manufacturer handling production.
brought: Kylie Jenner
Huge social audiences and a launch that felt like news.
Her partners
Manufacturing, fulfilment and, later, retail distribution.
turning_point: In November 2019 Coty bought 51% of her beauty business for $600 million, valuing it at about $1.2 billion. Questions were later raised about how large the business had been reported to be.
evidence: The deal is documented. Later reporting questioned earlier claims about revenue and wealth, so the purchase price is more reliable than earlier figures.
lesson: A launch run through the founder’s own channels can sell out with no traditional advertising. Lasting value needs the operations behind it.
take: Kylie Cosmetics is the case that made every celebrity think like a creator. The audience was the distribution, and the deal priced it.

title: The Show with Questions and Hot Wings
hook: Celebrities answered questions while eating ever-hotter wings. The hot sauces became a business of their own.
situation: Celebrity interviews followed a press-junket script. Online food channels mostly lived on advertising.
exchange: First We Feast launched Hot Ones in 2015, with Sean Evans interviewing guests while they ate wings with ten increasingly hot sauces. The show partnered with Heatonist to sell the sauces, then made its own, including The Last Dab.
brought: Sean Evans and First We Feast
Deep research, a format that made guests drop their guard and a recognisable set of sauces.
Heatonist
A hot sauce shop that made and sold the line.
turning_point: The sauces sold out repeatedly, and Digiday reported that First We Feast earned about 85% of its revenue outside advertising, much of it from products tied to the show.
metric_label: Share of First We Feast revenue from outside advertising, as reported
measure: A share reported by Digiday from company figures
evidence: Digiday’s reporting is specific about the revenue mix. Absolute figures were not published.
lesson: If the product is in every episode, sell it. A format with a signature object can be a shop as well as a show.
take: Hot Ones is the best example of a show whose props became the business. Every episode is an advert that nobody skips.
credit: First We Feast and Sean Evans, 2015

title: Hashtag United
hook: A YouTuber started a football team for his videos. It joined the real English league system and kept getting promoted.
situation: Football clubs have histories measured in decades. A team created for YouTube videos seemed like a novelty that would never play competitive football.
exchange: Spencer Owen founded Hashtag United in 2016 to play exhibition matches filmed for YouTube. In 2018 it joined the English football pyramid, with a fanbase built online.
brought: Spencer Owen
A YouTube audience and the idea that fans could follow a club from its first match.
The English football pyramid
A route from the lowest league upwards, open to any club that meets the rules.
turning_point: The club won promotions, reaching the Isthmian League by 2022, and launched a women’s team. A YouTube channel had become a real club with real fixtures.
metric_label: When Hashtag United joined the English football pyramid
measure: A date. Attendance and revenue are reported by the club in part
evidence: The club’s league history is documented by The Non-League Football Paper and others. Its commercial figures are not published in full.
lesson: Audiences will follow a creator into a real-world institution if they can belong to it. Membership is a stronger bond than viewing.
take: Hashtag United is my favourite British case in this edition. It took the oldest kind of community, a football club, and built one from a YouTube channel.

title: The Diary of a CEO
hook: A young entrepreneur started a podcast about running a company. It became Britain’s biggest podcast and the base of a media business.
situation: British podcasts were dominated by broadcasters and comedians. Long interviews with business leaders were seen as niche.
exchange: Steven Bartlett, co-founder of the agency Social Chain, launched The Diary of a CEO in 2017, then invested in filming it as a long-form video show for YouTube and building his own company, Flight Story, around it.
brought: Steven Bartlett
Interviews that went deep, and a business built to make and market them.
His guests and audience
Hours of conversation and an audience that watched on YouTube as much as it listened.
turning_point: Apple named it the UK’s number one podcast of 2024, it became the most subscribed podcast on YouTube’s charts, and it passed a billion views and downloads.
measure: A combined total of views and downloads announced by the show. Attention, not revenue
evidence: Apple’s ranking and the show’s milestones are documented. The revenue of Flight Story and related businesses is not public.
lesson: A show can be the front door to a company. Owning production, marketing and investment around it multiplies its value.
take: Bartlett treats the podcast as the top of a business funnel he owns. That is the creator-as-company model, built in Britain.

title: Chamberlain Coffee
hook: Her vlogs were full of iced coffee. So she started a coffee company, and learnt how hard retail is.
situation: Emma Chamberlain’s vlogs had changed YouTube’s style with quick edits and self-mocking honesty, and coffee was a running theme. Creator products were often merchandise rather than real consumer brands.
exchange: In 2019 she launched Chamberlain Coffee, selling online to her audience, then expanding into supermarkets and ready-to-drink cans and opening a café.
brought: Emma Chamberlain
A huge young audience and a personal connection to the product.
Investors and retailers
Funding and shelf space at Walmart, Target and others.
turning_point: The brand reached major retailers and became one of the best-known creator food brands. Reporting in 2024 described difficulty raising new money as it pushed to grow beyond her audience.
measure: A date. Revenue has been reported in estimates, not published
evidence: The brand’s growth and its fundraising challenges are documented by TechCrunch and The Ankler. Without published revenue, the case rests on the record of distribution.
lesson: An audience can launch a consumer brand, but shelf space has to be earned by rate of sale. Plan for the customers who have never seen the creator.
take: Chamberlain Coffee is the honest middle of the creator brand story. It shows that fame gets you into the shop and the product has to keep you there.

title: Sides
hook: Seven British YouTubers launched a fried chicken brand on delivery apps. Then they opened real restaurants.
situation: The Sidemen, a group including KSI, had one of Britain’s biggest YouTube audiences, with videos, charity football matches and merchandise. Virtual restaurant brands were booming during the pandemic.
exchange: In late 2021 the group launched Sides, a fried chicken brand sold through delivery kitchens, then opened their first restaurant at Boxpark Wembley in 2022, followed by more sites.
brought: The Sidemen
A young British audience that turned up in person, and constant promotion in their videos.
Restaurant partners
Kitchens, sites and the operations to serve food at scale.
turning_point: Sides grew from a delivery-only brand into a chain of physical sites in 2022, one of the first creator restaurant brands in Britain to make the move.
metric_label: When the first Sides restaurant opened, at Boxpark Wembley
measure: A date. Sales have not been published
evidence: The launch and openings are documented by Restaurant Online and others. Revenue is not public.
lesson: Test with delivery, then open where the audience lives. A creator restaurant needs an operator as good as its audience.
take: Sides is the British answer to MrBeast Burger, with a key difference: it moved slowly from delivery to sites with an operator. That patience is the lesson.

title: CrunchLabs
hook: A former NASA engineer made science videos for millions. Then he started posting kids a monthly box to build.
situation: Mark Rober’s engineering videos were among YouTube’s most watched, and widely used by parents and teachers. Science kits for children were sold by toy companies with little link to the creators children watched.
exchange: In 2022 Rober launched CrunchLabs, a subscription that sends a toy to build each month, with a video from him explaining the engineering behind it.
brought: Mark Rober
Trust with parents, a talent for explaining things and an audience of curious children.
The CrunchLabs team
Product design, manufacturing and subscription operations.
turning_point: CrunchLabs became a business that turned his videos into a product children use every month, later adding a more advanced robotics subscription.
measure: A date. Subscriber and revenue figures are not public
evidence: The launch and later products are documented by the company and trade press. Without published figures, the case rests on what was built.
lesson: Turn the thing the audience learns from you into a thing they can do. Products that extend the content are easier to sell than products that sit beside it.
take: CrunchLabs is the cleanest fit between a creator and a product in this edition. The box is the video, made physical.

title: Rhode
hook: A small skincare line sold almost entirely through its founder’s posts. Three years later it sold for a billion dollars.
situation: Celebrity beauty brands were crowded, and many struggled after launch. A brand with a handful of products seemed an unlikely acquisition target.
exchange: Hailey Bieber launched Rhode in June 2022 with a few products, sold online and promoted through her own posts and the get-ready videos of creators who liked them.
brought: Hailey Bieber
Her own audience, personal style and close involvement in the products.
e.l.f. Beauty
A buyer with retail scale and experience growing social-first brands.
turning_point: In May 2025 e.l.f. Beauty agreed to buy Rhode for up to $1 billion, including future payments, saying the brand had about $212 million in net sales in the previous year.
metric_label: Price agreed by e.l.f. Beauty, May 2025, including future payments
measure: The announced deal value, including an earn-out
evidence: The deal and Rhode’s sales were disclosed by e.l.f. and reported widely. Rhode is a celebrity-founded brand that behaved like a creator brand, which is why it belongs here.
deal_value: Up to $1 billion, including earn-out, May 2025
lesson: Fewer products, sold with real involvement, can beat a big range. Focus makes a creator brand easier to love and to buy.
take: Rhode proves the creator model now runs the beauty industry. The founder posts, creators copy, and the brand grows without a traditional campaign.
how_to_measure: For a founder-led brand, track sales from creator content the brand didn’t pay for, against paid content. The unpaid share shows real demand.

title: The Founders Buy It Back
hook: Two friends started a comedy channel in 2005 and sold it. Eighteen years later they bought it back.
situation: Smosh, one of YouTube’s first stars, had been sold to a media company, which collapsed in 2018. The brand was bought by Mythical Entertainment and kept going, but the founders no longer owned it.
exchange: In June 2023 Ian Hecox and Anthony Padilla, who had left in 2017, bought Smosh back from Mythical and returned to making it together.
brought: Ian Hecox and Anthony Padilla
The original creative partnership and a reason for old fans to come back.
Smosh’s cast and audience
A brand that had survived several owners and still had a large audience.
turning_point: The founders reunited on screen and Smosh signed with a major talent agency, positioning the brand for a new phase under creator ownership.
metric_label: When the founders bought Smosh back
measure: A date. The price was not disclosed
evidence: The purchase is documented by Tubefilter and others. Terms were not published.
lesson: Creator brands are worth most in the hands of the people who made them. Investors in creator companies should plan for the founders, not around them.
take: Smosh appears in Edition 02 as the top name in a 2014 survey. Its story closes the loop on ownership: built by creators, sold, broken and bought back by the creators who started it.
credit: Ian Hecox and Anthony Padilla, 2005 to 2023
impact_source: Read about the agency signing · Yahoo
how_to_measure: After a change of ownership, track the return of lapsed viewers and the share of revenue from products and live events the founders control.

title: Trick Shots, Then a Nine-Figure Deal
hook: College friends filmed basketball trick shots in a back garden. Fifteen years later investors put in more than $100 million.
situation: Dude Perfect started in 2009 with trick-shot videos and grew into one of YouTube’s biggest sports entertainment channels, with live tours, merchandise and a family audience. Creators rarely raised outside capital at that scale.
exchange: In 2024 the five founders took more than $100 million from Highmount Capital to build the company beyond YouTube, into new shows, live events and a physical headquarters for fans.
brought: Dude Perfect
Fifteen years of family-friendly content and a brand parents trusted.
Highmount Capital
Capital and backing to grow into a wider entertainment company.
turning_point: The deal was the first institutional investment in the company and one of the largest in a creator business. It treated a YouTube channel as an entertainment company with a long future.
measure: The investment amount reported by the company and the press
evidence: The investment is documented by Fox Business, Tubefilter and others. The valuation and revenue were not disclosed.
lesson: Investors back creator companies that own a format, a brand and an audience across ages. Family trust is an asset with a long life.
take: Dude Perfect closes the edition because it shows where creator brands are going: from videos, to products, to companies that raise money like any other.
